title: The Third Letter of John
lead: The shortest book of the New Testament in Greek words (219 in the SBL text; 2 John has 245): a personal letter from "the Elder" to Gaius, praising him for receiving traveling brothers who went out "for the sake of the Name," and complaining of Diotrephes, "who loves to be first," who will not welcome the Elder's people and drives out of the church those who do. It is the only book of the New Testament that never names Jesus or Christ, and it shows the travel, hospitality and quarrels of the churches at the end of the first century.

sections.b: Greeting and the wish for Gaius' health (1:1-4); praise for his help to the traveling brothers, "strangers at that," and the call to send them on in a way worthy of God (1:5-8); Diotrephes, who rejected the Elder's letter and his people (1:9-10); "do not imitate the bad, but the good," and the good word for Demetrius (1:11-12); a visit hoped for, and greetings to "the friends," each by name (1:13-14).

Nothing is known of Gaius, Diotrephes or Demetrius beyond this letter; the much later Apostolic Constitutions make Gaius a bishop of Pergamum and Demetrius a bishop of Philadelphia. Whether Diotrephes was an early single bishop (Adolf von Harnack), a local leader in a quarrel over authority rather than doctrine (C. H. Dodd), or the man who refused 2 John (John Painter) is debated; the chapter page sets out the readings. 3 John 2 has been read as a promise of health and wealth (Oral Roberts) and as an ordinary letter-writer's wish for a friend's health.
